source.text: Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν σικυηράτῳ προβασκάνιον οὐδὲν φυλάσσον, οὕτως οἱ θεοὶ αὐτῶν εἰσὶν ξύλινοι καὶ περίχρυσοι καὶ περιάργυροι.
source.note: Swete volume III, third edition (1905), printed p. 384 / one-based PDF p. 408 / zero-based scan leaf 407. translation.text: For just as a scarecrow in a cucumber patch guards nothing[a], so their gods are wooden and overlaid with gold and silver.

footnotes.text: Or 'protective charm.' The Greek names a protective object, here one that guards nothing.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a place planted with cucumbers or gourds. 'Cucumber patch' is the most natural and specific English rendering, while preserving the agricultural image familiar from Greek usage and LXX parallels.

The printed Greek has a neuter noun naming a protective object, followed by the agreeing participle φυλάσσον and its object οὐδέν. The field context supports scarecrow; the protective-charm range remains in the note. The earlier malformed transcription and explanation as an unwatched patch are superseded.

The neuter participle agrees with προβασκάνιον; οὐδέν is its object. The English finite clause preserves the comparison: the protective figure guards nothing, rather than the noun disappearing into an unguarded field.
The Greek says 'gods,' reflecting the polemical claim about what 'their gods' are. 'Idols' would interpret rather than translate the lexical form.
A straightforward adjectival rendering preserves the material description and the mocking tone of the verse.
The compound indicates being covered around with gold rather than being solid gold. 'Overlaid with gold' is precise and clear in modern English.
As with περίχρυσοι, the sense is covered with silver. 'Overlaid with silver' keeps the parallel structure and material emphasis.

theological_decisions.issue: Whether to translate θεοὶ as 'gods' or interpretively as 'idols' in this anti-idolatry context
theological_decisions.rationale: The text itself uses the term 'gods' as part of its polemic, then immediately defines their material nature. Retaining 'gods' preserves the rhetoric of the source without importing an interpretive substitute.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §1, original-language primacy over translation tradition

footnotes.text: The Greek phrase rendered 'there is nothing guarding it' is textually and lexically difficult; the sense is that the cucumber patch is left unprotected or unwatched.

The transmitted form is difficult, but in context it conveys lack of protection or watchfulness. The phrase is rendered idiomatically as 'there is nothing guarding it' to reflect the sense of an unprotected field without overcommitting to a more specific reconstruction not explicit in the source witness.
φυλάσσω commonly means to guard or keep watch. 'Guarding' fits the agricultural comparison and pairs naturally with the preceding negative sense.

source.text: τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ τῇ ἐν κήπῳ ῥάμνῳ, ἐφ’ ἧς πᾶν τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπικάθηται, ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ νεκρῷ ἐρριμμένῳ ἐν σκότει ἀφωμοίωνται οἱ θεοὶ αὐτῶν ξύλινοι καὶ περίχρυσοι καὶ περιάργυροι.
source.note: Swete volume III, third edition (1905), printed p. 384 / one-based PDF p. 408 / zero-based scan leaf 407. Selected printed text checked for this complete verse; legacy edition identifier retained. This corrects POB transcription, not an ancient manuscript emendation or historical-priority judgment.

translation.text: In the same way, their wooden gods overlaid with gold and silver are like a thornbush[a] in a garden, on which every bird sits, and also like a dead body thrown out in the dark.

footnotes.text: Greek names a thorny shrub; 'buckthorn' is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Idiomatic introductory phrase marking comparison; 'In the same way' is natural modern English and preserves the comparative force.

The printed dative is ῥάμνῳ, a thorny shrub, not the malformed βάμψῳ. LSJ includes several prickly shrubs, so thornbush avoids an unsupported species identification. This is a second comparison, distinct from the protective figure in verse 69.
κήπος commonly means 'garden'; no contextual need to narrow to orchard.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ἐφ’ ἧς πᾶν τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπικάθηται
lexical_decisions.rationale: Straightforward relative clause; 'sits' is simple and natural, while still reflecting the image of birds perching on an inert object.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a dead body thrown out in the dark
alternatives: the dead one lying discarded in darkness
lexical_decisions.rationale: νεκρός here is best rendered concretely as 'dead body/corpse.' ἐρριμμένῳ conveys being thrown or cast aside. 'In the dark' preserves ἐν σκότει without overinterpreting it as metaphysical darkness.
The perfect passive expresses a comparison or likeness. Are like is idiomatic English here, not a claim that the gods were physically remade into a shrub or corpse.

lexical_decisions.source_word: οἱ θεοὶ αὐτῶν ξύλινοι καὶ περίχρυσοι καὶ περιάργυροι
lexical_decisions.chosen: their wooden gods overlaid with gold and silver
alternatives: their gods of wood, covered with gold and silver
their wooden gods plated with gold and silver
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξύλινοι identifies the idols as wooden in substance; περίχρυσοι and περιάργυροι indicate gold and silver covering/overlay. 'Overlaid with gold and silver' is clear and idiomatic.

theological_decisions.issue: Preserving the two comparisons in the selected Greek text
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: The gods are compared to a thornbush on which birds sit and to a discarded corpse.
alternative_readings: Buckthorn is a possible narrower rendering of the shrub.
theological_decisions.rationale: The shrub image must not be harmonized into the preceding scarecrow. A thornbush is not literally lifeless; the anti-idol rhetoric does not authorize replacing the stated plant with an inert watch-figure. This correction does not decide literary dependence, an original Hebrew text, or canonical status.

translation.text: In the same way[a], their wooden gods overlaid with gold and silver are made like a scarecrow in a garden, on which every bird sits, and also like a dead body thrown out in the dark.

footnotes.text: Or 'a post/watch-figure in a garden.' The Greek term is rare, and the image is of an object set up in a garden on which birds freely perch.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Idiomatic introductory phrase marking comparison; 'In the same way' is natural modern English and preserves the comparative force.

In context 'the one in a garden, on which every bird sits' refers to a bird-scaring figure or post set up in a garden. 'Scarecrow' best conveys the image for modern readers, though the Greek term is unusual and may denote a garden post/figure more literally.
κήπος commonly means 'garden'; no contextual need to narrow to orchard.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ἐφ’ ἧς πᾶν τὸ ὄρνεον ἐπικάθηται
lexical_decisions.rationale: Straightforward relative clause; 'sits' is simple and natural, while still reflecting the image of birds perching on an inert object.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a dead body thrown out in the dark
alternatives: the dead one lying discarded in darkness
lexical_decisions.rationale: νεκρός here is best rendered concretely as 'dead body/corpse.' ἐρριμμένῳ conveys being thrown or cast aside. 'In the dark' preserves ἐν σκότει without overinterpreting it as metaphysical darkness.
The verb expresses comparison or assimilation. 'Are made like' keeps the passive/comparative sense and fits the sentence structure.

lexical_decisions.source_word: οἱ θεοὶ αὐτῶν ξύλινοι καὶ περίχρυσοι καὶ περιάργυροι
lexical_decisions.chosen: their wooden gods overlaid with gold and silver
alternatives: their gods of wood, covered with gold and silver
their wooden gods plated with gold and silver
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξύλινοι identifies the idols as wooden in substance; περίχρυσοι and περιάργυροι indicate gold and silver covering/overlay. 'Overlaid with gold and silver' is clear and idiomatic.

theological_decisions.issue: Nature of the comparison in an anti-idolatry context
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: The verse compares idols to lifeless, useless objects: a garden scarecrow/post and a discarded corpse.
alternative_readings: The garden image could be rendered more literally as a garden post or watch-figure rather than 'scarecrow'.
theological_decisions.rationale: The theology of the verse is polemical against idols as powerless and inert. The translation preserves that force without adding interpretive expansion beyond the imagery present in the Greek.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy: original-language primacy; preserve theological tension rather than resolve it
